In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of in vitro tissue specimens is not a satisfactory substitute for the study of tissue specimens taken in situ.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

X‐ray microanalytical measurements of tissue slices can be performed without any major changes in the intracelluar ionic concentrations, provided that the tissue is incubated in a fluid resembling the extracelluar compartment in its ion content and that incubation temperature and duration are kept low.
the use of post mortem tissue specimens for X-ray microanalysis is feasible, provided that the tissue is dissected and incubated under strictly defined conditions.
the use of in vitro preparations for X‐ray‐microanalysis is justified, provided that the effects of dissection and incubated in a physiological solution are considered.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in vitro tissue slices can be used to investigate physiological changes of intracellular ion concentrations, as long as the dissection and incubational procedures are carefully standardized.

in vitro tissue slices, if prepared and incubated in a suitable way, are suitable for studies of physiological changes of intracellular ion concentrations, and that X‐ray microanalytical data obtained on such slices can be used for comparison with data obtained in vivo.
, in order to obtain reliable data by X‐ray analysis of tissue, it is necessary to keep the tissue as undisturbed as possible, and to use a buffer that resembles the extracellular fluid.
